title: Moon sighting debates
hook: calculation or sighting, local or global, still debated

segments.voice: Yesterday, social media and the tongue: say good, or keep silent. Your line was the tongue has thumbs. Did anything stay unposted? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

It's the twenty-ninth night of Ramadan, and the family group chat is busy. One mosque has announced: Eid is tomorrow. Another, across town, says: not yet, we fast one more day. An aunt forwards a sighting from another country. A cousin posts an astronomy chart. Somebody asks, half joking, whether the family is allowed to have two Eids. Nobody in the chat is being careless. Every one of them is trying to do the same thing, start the feast on the right day. Today is about why the same thin crescent can be read so many ways, and where those readings come from.
screen: `TWO MOSQUES, TWO ANSWERS.` → `A SIGHTING FROM ABROAD.` → `ONE CRESCENT, READ MANY WAYS.`

segments.voice: Begin with the Qur'an. People asked the Prophet about the new moons, and the answer, in Pickthall's translation, is: "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage." The moon is the calendar. The verse doesn't say how to read it. That comes from the hadith. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: fast when you see it, and end the fast when you see it, and if it is hidden from you, complete thirty days. In another report he says his community does not write or calculate, and the month is sometimes this long and sometimes that, shown with his hands. Here is the first debate. Some scholars read these words as a command: the month begins with a human eye seeing the crescent. Others read the mention of not calculating as a description of that time, and accept astronomical calculation now that it can be done. Then the second debate, and it has a story. Imam Muslim records that a man named Kurayb was in Syria at the start of Ramadan. There they saw the new moon on Friday night. He came back to Medina and told Ibn 'Abbas, who said: we saw it on Saturday night, and we'll keep fasting until we complete thirty or see it ourselves. Kurayb asked, isn't the sighting in Syria enough? Ibn 'Abbas said no; this is how the Messenger of Allah commanded us. So some communities follow a local sighting. Others accept a sighting from anywhere, so that one sighting starts the month for everyone. Others follow calculation. Each can point to something in the sources. None of them is ignoring the moon.
screen: `THE NEW MOONS: FIXED SEASONS.` · `FAST WHEN YOU SEE IT.` · `SIGHTING OR CALCULATION?` · `KURAYB: SYRIA SAW IT FIRST.` · then, large: `LOCAL OR GLOBAL?`

segments.voice: The practice: one moon, held kindly. Settle, and breathe. Picture a thin crescent low over the horizon just after sunset, so faint you'd have to know where to look. Now picture the people looking for it: someone on a rooftop, someone with a telescope, someone reading a table of numbers, someone waiting for a phone call from abroad. All of them facing the same sky. Notice whether any of them annoys you. Let that go with the breath. If you pray, you can remember the people who will be fasting or feasting on a different day from you. The bell holds the time.
Moon sighting debates. Seeing with the eye or calculating, one local sighting or one for everyone: questions Muslims still weigh about when a month begins. Today's word.

Your line: one moon, many views. Today, find out how your local mosque or a community near you decides when the month begins. Tomorrow, prayer times in the far north. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Muslim communities decide the start of Ramadan and the Eids in different ways: some wait for a local sighting of the crescent, some accept a sighting from another country, and some follow astronomical calculation.

myth: the Qur'an spells out exactly how to sight the moon
2:189 calls the new moons fixed seasons; the method comes from the hadith and how scholars read it.
in Sahih Muslim, Ibn 'Abbas did not follow the sighting from Syria
he told Kurayb they would fast until they completed thirty or saw it themselves.
the hadith says that if the moon is hidden, complete thirty days
fast when you see it, end the fast when you see it, and if it's hidden, complete thirty.

fork.setup: you're Ibn 'Abbas in Medina. Kurayb arrives from Syria: they saw the new moon a night before you did. what do you do?
options: adopt the Syrian date at once.
keep to your own sighting and complete the month.
ask the astronomers to settle it.
fork.reveal: he kept to Medina's sighting and said this is how the Messenger of Allah commanded them. some scholars build the case for local sighting on this report; others read it differently.

original.note: Arabic: the new crescent moon; 2:189 uses its plural.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims can't agree because nobody checked the moon.
what it means: everyone is checking; the debate is over how, by eye or by calculation, and whose sighting counts, local or global.
what a scholar hears: 2:189 on the new moons, the hadith 'fast when you see it' in al-Bukhari, and Kurayb's report in Sahih Muslim, read by some for local sighting.

sources.quoted: They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1909 (fast when you see it; if hidden, complete thirty)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1913 (we neither write nor calculate; the month is like this and like this)

notes: Confirm Pickthall's exact wording and punctuation of 2:189 (opening clause).
Confirm hadith numbers: Bukhari 1909, 1913; Muslim 1087. In 1909 the thirty days refer to completing Sha'ban; the script says 'complete thirty days' without naming the month.
Kurayb's report: Syria saw it on Friday night, Medina on Saturday night, per Sahih Muslim; confirm days.
The three approaches (local sighting, a sighting from anywhere, calculation) are described without naming any council or country; a Keeper may add named examples.
The hook's 'twenty-ninth night' is the script's scene, consistent with the hadith that a month can be cut short; no statistic is implied.

Editor: the 2:189 quotation is trimmed to the answer clause only, since the punctuation of Pickthall's opening clause ('of new moons, say:') was uncertain; the fork's anachronistic 'calculator' became 'astronomers'.
